question: Drugs causing hypokalemia are : a) Amphotericin B b) Insulin c) Cyclosporine d) Carbenoxolone e) NSAIDs
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Amphotericin B" -> "renal tubular damage" -> "increased potassium excretion" -> "hypokalemia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Insulin" -> "cellular uptake of potassium" -> "decreased serum potassium" -> "hypokalemia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Cyclosporine" -> "possible renal effects" -> "unclear impact on potassium" -> 50%
CHAIN: "NSAIDs" -> "renal effects" -> "possible potassium retention" -> "unclear impact on hypokalemia" -> 40%
analysis: To determine which drugs cause hypokalemia, we need to consider their mechanisms of action and effects on potassium levels. Amphotericin B is well-documented to cause hypokalemia due to its nephrotoxic effects, leading to increased renal potassium excretion. Insulin can cause hypokalemia by driving potassium into cells, thus lowering serum potassium levels. Carbenoxolone, due to its mineralocorticoid-like effects, can also lead to hypokalemia by promoting renal potassium excretion. Cyclosporine is not typically associated with hypokalemia; it can sometimes cause hyperkalemia instead. NSAIDs are more likely to cause hyperkalemia due to their effects on renal function and potassium retention. Therefore, the drugs most consistently associated with hypokalemia are Amphotericin B, Insulin, and Carbenoxolone, supporting option 'opd. acd'.
